newsitem.title: USA: U.S. junk bond funds cash flows turned negative.
newsitem.headline: U.S. junk bond funds cash flows turned negative.

text.p: For the first time in 1997, weekly net cash flows into U.S. high-yield mutual funds turned negative, according to AMG Data Services.
Investors pulled $316.5 million out of U.S. high-yield mutual funds for the week ended March 19, according to AMG Data Services.

"The outflows have already been reflected by selling over the past week," said one high-yield trader. "But it sort of worries poeple when they see it in print. I would think the market will be down (on this news)," he said.
Mark Durbiano, who manages $2.8 billion in high-yield investments at Federated Investors, said this week's outflows are still the result of market-timer investor activity.
Based on activity he has he seen in his owns funds, Durbiano said, "The core retail customer continues to be an investor (in high-yield funds)."
Market timers are specialized money managers who are known for making large market moves based on price momentum.
"They tend to operate in short, large bursts of activity. We are probably in the midst of this. They should come back when price momentum starts to turn around," he said.

High-yield mutual funds managed by Zurich Kemper Investments, Strong Capital Management, Putnam Investments, Federated Investors, Janus Capital Corp and PIMCO Advisors LP were among those that saw the highest rate of outflows, confirmed Bob Adler, president of AMG.
Junk bond players said these funds were popular among market-timer investors.
Inflows into high-yield mutual funds began to slow several weeks ago after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan suggested that the high-yield bond market may be overvalued, experts said.
Prior to that, investors had been pouring near record amounts of new cash into junk-bond funds.
The last time high-yield mutual funds experienced weekly outflows was October 16, 1996, Adler said.

Adler said the rate of inflows into junk bonds, as measured by a four-week moving average, has declined by more than half from a peak of $526 million on February 26. Last week's four-week moving average was $229 million.
Despite outflows among junk-bond funds, investment-grade and high-quality corporate bond funds continued to show inflows last week, Adler noted.
AMG, based in Arcata, California, is a U.S. mutual fund information company.
